name: Karl Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Karl. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and we don't sell anything. What you say is confidential. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the surface-mount line at an electronics plant on the business park, making circuit boards for boiler controls and heating thermostats. My job is loading the reels of tiny components into the pick-and-place machine, which is a robot that puts thousands of parts on each board, then watching the boards go through the reflow oven and pulling any that the camera flags. Two years in, and I still get the reel feeders mixed up sometimes, which stops the line and gets me a look from Priya, the line lead. The work's clean and quiet compared to what I used to do.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you used to do?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Chef, for nearly twenty years, the last six as sous chef in a hotel kitchen. Sixty-hour weeks, burns up my arms, and I missed most of Hugo's first years. When I was 41 I just stopped, and a mate got me in here. I actually like the precision of it, it's a bit like mise en place, everything in its place before service. I use the AI on my phone all day, mostly to look up part numbers and error codes faster than the manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, it's a handy tool, not a miracle. I'd probably post something in the old chefs' group chat, because they were all convinced robots would be flipping burgers by now. Then I'd carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it changes nothing for me, which is fine. My job's already half robot, I'm the bloke who feeds it and watches it. If it stays this way, I'll just get better at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to train on the machine programming side, setting up new board jobs, which pays more. I'd keep our savings ticking along, we've got about four months put by. Maybe do a weekend course in electronics basics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Bit bored, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Would anything change for you if it's mostly hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd still use it. It saves me twenty minutes a shift on part numbers alone. Priya's started asking me to look things up for her, which is funny, given I'm the junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you want to be in a few years, in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Line programmer, maybe even process technician. I like knowing why things work. And home by six every night, which after kitchens still feels like a holiday.

S0.say: It's a handy tool, not a miracle. He'd post something in his old chefs' group chat, because they were sure robots would be flipping burgers by now, and then carry on.
S0.think: It changes nothing for him, which is fine, since his job is already half robot. If it stays this way, he'll just get better at feeding and watching the machine.
S0.do: Asks to train on programming new board jobs, which pays more, and may take a weekend electronics course. Keeps adding to the family's four months of savings.
S0.feel: Calm, and maybe a bit bored.
S0.quote: Priya's started asking me to look things up for her, which is funny, given I'm the junior.
S0.fieldNote: Karl already works alongside a robot and uses AI daily, so a plateau barely registers. His pride in being the junior who becomes the go-to for lookups was clear. His life measure is getting home by six, which he treasures after his kitchen years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shift, and the people who learn the tools will do fine. I'd also say companies should help, because not everyone can learn on their phone at midnight like I do. Both are true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm one of the lucky ones. The loading and checking gets automated, sure, but someone has to set up the new jobs and fix it when it's wrong. I want to be that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the manager in the first month and ask to train as a process technician. I'd do an online course in electronics and the basics of programming the line, evenings, about three hours a week. I'd use the AI to help me study, I already do for most things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, actually. Even a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should pay for the retraining you mentioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of both. The company gets the savings, so they should pay for the training. But if I can learn on my own I won't wait for them. Waiting is how people get left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone on the line you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stan, on the next machine. He's fifty-eight and he's been there thirty years, and he still writes everything on a notepad. I'd try to help him, but he doesn't want help.

S1.say: People who learn the tools will do fine, but companies should help, because not everyone can study on their phone at midnight. He'd say both are true.
S1.think: He thinks he's one of the lucky ones, because someone has to set up the new jobs and fix the line when it goes wrong. He wants to be that person.
S1.do: Asks his manager in the first month to train as a process technician. Takes an evening online course in electronics and line programming for about three hours a week, using AI to help him study.
S1.feel: Pretty calm, even a bit excited.
S1.quote: Waiting is how people get left behind.
S1.fieldNote: Karl sees steady change as a chance to climb rather than a threat. His centrist view splits responsibility between companies and individuals, but in practice he won't wait. His concern for an older colleague who refuses help showed empathy alongside his confidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, and governments and companies need to work out quickly how people get paid. No point pretending it isn't happening. I'd say it calmly, though, because panic doesn't help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think even the technician job goes if the AI can fix the line itself. I'd have a year or two of being useful, then I'm in the same boat as everyone. That worries me more than I'd show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself the person who knows the new systems best and hang on as long as I could. We'd save hard, maybe three hundred a month, and I'd start doing weekend catering, private dinners and parties, for cash. People still want a real cook at a birthday, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but a lot more than I let on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, does the technician plan still work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for long. I'd learn it anyway, because a year of good pay is a year of good pay. But I'd stop thinking of it as a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You were a chef for twenty years. Does that come back into it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's my backup. The robots might make better chips than me, but a sixtieth birthday party wants someone in the kitchen telling stories. I'd start building that up straight away, word of mouth, a little website.

S2.say: It's a shock, and governments and companies need to work out quickly how people get paid. He'd say it calmly, because panic doesn't help anyone.
S2.think: Even the technician job goes if AI can fix the line itself, so he'd have a year or two of usefulness before he's in the same boat as everyone. That worries him more than he shows.
S2.do: Becomes the person who knows the new systems best to hang on longer. Saves about three hundred a month and starts weekend catering for private dinners and parties, built through word of mouth and a small website.
S2.feel: Anxious, a lot more than he lets on, though not panicking.
S2.quote: The robots might make better chips than me, but a sixtieth birthday party wants someone in the kitchen telling stories.
S2.fieldNote: His old trade suddenly becomes a fallback, built on the personal touch rather than the food. He would still learn the technician skills for short-term pay. His calm public line covers real private worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready, so get ready. Learn the tools, save money, think about what people will still want from a person. That's what I'd tell my mates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to get the technician job, earn better money for a couple of years, and build the catering on the side. Then when it arrives, I've got savings and a second thing. I think I'd be okay, but I'm not certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Technician training in year one, saving the extra pay, maybe three hundred a month. Catering at weekends starting small, maybe twice a month. I'd ask the AI to help with the business side, costings and that, because that's where I'm weakest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. Like before a busy service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having five years change, compared to two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to build the second thing properly, so it's not a desperate scramble. With two years I'd be cooking at weekends just to pay the mortgage. With five I can grow it slowly and see if it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Annika feel about you cooking at weekends again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be wary. She remembers the kitchen years, the missed bedtimes. I'd have to promise it's twice a month, not every weekend, and keep that promise.

S3.say: There's time to get ready, so get ready: learn the tools, save money and think about what people will still want from a person. That's what he'd tell his mates.
S3.think: Five years is enough to get the technician job, earn better money and build catering on the side. When it arrives, he'd have savings and a second income, and he thinks he'd be okay, though not certain.
S3.do: Starts technician training in year one and saves the extra pay, about three hundred a month. Starts weekend catering twice a month and uses AI for costings and the business side.
S3.feel: Uneasy but mostly fine, like the nerves before a busy service.
S3.quote: With two years I'd be cooking at weekends just to pay the mortgage.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time turns his catering from an emergency fallback into a slowly grown second income. His wife's memories of his kitchen years are a real limit he takes seriously. He knows business planning is his weak point and would lean on AI there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if you use it. Plan, save, learn. And don't listen to anyone who says it'll never happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels like enough to set things up properly. Technician for a few years, savings, catering growing, and maybe something more by the end. I'd be 53 and I'd want to be my own boss by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same start: technician training and saving. Then around year five, I'd put some savings into proper catering kit or a small unit, if the weekends are going well. I'd also put a bit into a pension fund or shares, because if robots make all the money, I want a small piece.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the low kind. Mostly I'm curious how it plays out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you do anything bigger than weekend catering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a small food business, a lunch place or events catering, run with a couple of people. I'd use whatever tools are around to do the boring bits. The cooking and the talking I'd keep for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Hugo and Lena about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to do something with your hands and something with people. And learn to use the tools, whatever they are by then. Lena's seven, she'll grow up with it all, which is a strange thought.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift if you use it to plan, save and learn. He'd tell people not to listen to anyone who says it will never happen.
S4.think: Ten years feels like enough to set things up properly, from technician work to a growing catering business. He'd want to be his own boss by 53.
S4.do: Trains as a technician and saves, then around year five invests savings in catering equipment or a small unit if weekends go well. Puts some money into a pension fund or shares.
S4.feel: A low-level unease, mostly outweighed by curiosity.
S4.quote: The cooking and the talking I'd keep for me.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Karl plans to own something rather than work for someone, combining his chef past with his new technical skills. He wants a small stake in AI-driven wealth through shares. His advice to his children mixes hands, people and tools.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time to build a second thing, you just grab whatever's there. What would help is some kind of income floor while people retrain, and cheap loans or grants for people starting small businesses. And honest information about which jobs are actually lasting, not guesses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people want to keep. I left kitchens because they were killing me, not because I hated cooking. If robots take the bits that hurt and leave the bits we love, that's not a bad deal, as long as we can still pay the mortgage.

headlineQuote: I left kitchens because they were killing me, not because I hated cooking.
portrait: Karl Tanaka, 43, loads the pick-and-place robot on a circuit board line after nearly twenty years as a chef, and uses AI every day to look up parts faster than the manual. He is pragmatic about who should pay for change but won't wait for anyone, planning to become a process technician. Steady change leaves him calm, even excited, while fast AGI makes him anxious and turns his old cooking skills into a fallback. With five or ten years he grows weekend catering into a possible business of his own and puts a little into shares.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be no time to build a second source of income, only grabbing whatever is there.
whatWouldHelp: An income floor while people retrain, cheap loans or grants for small businesses, and honest information about which jobs are actually lasting.
